doc.title: Jackie McLean — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
title: Acting with the Living Theater and Julian Beck
summary: McLean understudied for Living Theater parts, played a Chinese bartender in Paris, and remembers Julian Beck making him up.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: I don’t know. This is not in a way funny, but you’re funny, you doing this. Have you done any more – other than the thing with Jack Gelber, have you done any other acting or put that part of yourself . . . ?

No. I never got a chance to. I always wanted to. When I was with the Living Theater, they saw that I was very interested in acting and that whole thing. So they always kept me as an understudy for any part. So we’d be like in France or something like that, and one of the guys who was an actor in the play got mad. We were over in Paris, and he said, “Aw, the hell with it. I’m going home.” He was playing a Chinese bartender in one of Bertolt Brecht’s plays or something in the city, or – I can’t think of the name of it, the name of the play they were doing. But right away, Judith Malina came to me and said, “Look, Jackie, you’re going to have to take his place. So here’s his lines. We’re going to make you up. You’re going to be a Chinese bartender. You’re going to have to do that too for us.” So I said okay. So every night . . .
So this was a repertory situation.
It wasn’t just The Connection that you were doing.
They were doing a variety of pieces.

Other plays as well. Waiting for Godot or one of those plays. I had a few lines. I had to run out and say something – “The stockyards are on fire” – as a Japanese or Chinese guy. They made me up and gave me all the makeup and stuff, pigtail hanging down and everything. I liked that. I enjoyed being in that company. Julian Beck. He always made me up every night.
What kind of guy was he?

Very talented, brilliant, brilliant theater man. He started out building sets. That was his first introduction to theater. Then he just grew and became swallowed up, because it can do that to you. It did it to me. I was very involved and very loving to be in the theater.
Were there particular thinkers or writers or others that you came to know through that community of people?

Yeah, but a lot of them were young actors that would later go on to be very famous, like the one that played in Godfather. He was around there, sweeping floors and moping and carrying on when I was in the Living Theater. The one that played the son in The Godfather. What’s his name? Michael, who went away to the Army and came back. You know The Godfather.
Anyway, him and a few other actors there.
No, I was still dealing with my megillah at that time.
